items.title: FATF Recommendation 1 - Risk-based approach
items.text: Institutions should identify, assess and understand money-laundering and terrorist-financing risks and apply measures commensurate with those risks: enhanced measures where risk is higher, simplified measures may be permitted where risk is demonstrably lower.

items.title: FATF Recommendation 10 - Customer due diligence
items.text: Institutions must identify the customer and verify identity using reliable, independent source documents, data or information; identify and take reasonable measures to verify the beneficial owner; understand the purpose and intended nature of the business relationship; and conduct ongoing due diligence. Where CDD cannot be completed, the relationship should not be opened and a suspicious transaction report should be considered.

items.title: FATF Recommendation 11 - Record keeping
items.text: Records obtained through CDD, account files and business correspondence should be kept for at least five years after the business relationship ends, and transaction records for at least five years after the transaction, sufficient to permit reconstruction and to be made available to competent authorities swiftly.

items.title: FATF Recommendation 12 - Politically exposed persons
items.text: For foreign PEPs (and domestic PEPs where higher risk), institutions should have risk-management systems to determine PEP status, obtain senior-management approval to establish the relationship, establish source of wealth and source of funds, and conduct enhanced ongoing monitoring.

items.title: FATF Recommendation 6 - Targeted financial sanctions
items.text: Institutions must screen customers against designated-persons lists and freeze without delay funds or assets of designated persons, and must not make funds available to them.

items.title: FATF Recommendation 15 - New technologies
items.text: Institutions should assess ML/TF risks of new products, business practices and delivery mechanisms, including non-face-to-face and digital onboarding, before launch, and take measures to manage and mitigate those risks.

items.title: FATF Recommendation 20 - Reporting of suspicious transactions
items.text: If an institution suspects or has reasonable grounds to suspect funds are proceeds of crime or related to terrorist financing, it must promptly report to the financial intelligence unit. Tipping-off the customer is prohibited.

items.title: FATF Guidance on Digital Identity
items.text: Reliable, independent digital ID systems with appropriate assurance levels for identity proofing and authentication can be used for CDD in non-face-to-face onboarding; institutions should understand the assurance level and governance of the digital ID system relied upon.

items.title: RBI Master Direction - Know Your Customer (KYC) Direction, 2016 (as amended)
items.text: Regulated entities must have a board-approved KYC policy covering customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification procedures and monitoring of transactions; identify customers using officially valid documents or equivalent e-documents, Aadhaar-based e-KYC where permitted, or digital KYC; categorise customers by risk; and identify beneficial owners of legal-entity customers.

items.title: RBI KYC Direction - Video-based Customer Identification Process (V-CIP)
items.text: V-CIP must be conducted by a trained official of the regulated entity through a live, real-time, consent-based audio-visual interaction with liveness checks, geo-tagging of the customer's location within the country, face matching against the identity document, and secure storage of the recorded session with date-time stamp; the process must be auditable and the infrastructure must meet prescribed security standards.

items.title: RBI KYC Direction - Periodic updation of KYC
items.text: KYC must be periodically updated on a risk basis: at least once every two years for high-risk customers, once every eight years for medium-risk customers and once every ten years for low-risk customers.

items.title: RBI KYC Direction - Central KYC Records Registry (CKYCR)
items.text: Regulated entities must upload KYC records of new individual and legal-entity customers to the Central KYC Records Registry within the prescribed timeline, and use the KYC identifier to retrieve records where the customer provides it.

items.title: Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002 and PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005
items.text: Reporting entities must verify client identity, maintain records of transactions and identity for five years after the relationship ends or the transaction, and furnish cash-transaction and suspicious-transaction reports to FIU-IND within prescribed timelines through a designated principal officer.

items.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
items.text: Personal data may be processed for a lawful purpose with consent following an itemised notice, or for certain legitimate uses including compliance with law. Data fiduciaries must implement reasonable security safeguards, notify the Data Protection Board and affected data principals of breaches, honour access, correction and erasure rights, and erase data when the purpose is served unless retention is required by law.

items.title: EU Anti-Money Laundering Directive (EU) 2015/849 as amended, and AML Regulation (EU) 2024/1624
items.text: Obliged entities must apply CDD including identification and verification of customers and beneficial owners (electronic identification means under eIDAS are acceptable), apply enhanced due diligence for high-risk third countries and PEPs, and retain CDD records for five years after the end of the relationship.

items.title: GDPR Articles 5-6 - Principles and lawful basis
items.text: Personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently, collected for specified purposes, adequate and limited to what is necessary, accurate, kept no longer than necessary and secured. KYC processing typically relies on the legal-obligation basis.

items.title: GDPR Article 9 - Special categories (biometric data)
items.text: Biometric data processed to uniquely identify a person is special-category data; processing requires a condition such as explicit consent or a specific legal basis, with appropriate safeguards.

items.title: GDPR Article 22 - Automated individual decision-making
items.text: Individuals have the right not to be subject to decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect them, subject to exceptions; where exceptions apply, safeguards include the right to obtain human intervention, express a view and contest the decision.

items.title: GDPR Articles 25, 32, 33 and 35 - Privacy by design, security, breach notification, DPIA
items.text: Controllers must implement data protection by design and by default, appropriate technical and organisational security measures such as encryption and pseudonymisation, notify the supervisory authority of personal-data breaches within 72 hours where feasible, and carry out a DPIA for high-risk processing.

items.title: US Customer Identification Program rule (31 CFR 1020.220)
items.text: Banks must implement a written CIP that, at minimum, collects name, date of birth, address and an identification number before opening an account, verifies identity within a reasonable time through documentary or non-documentary methods, keeps records, and checks government lists.

items.title: US FinCEN Customer Due Diligence Rule (31 CFR 1010.230)
items.text: Covered institutions must identify and verify the beneficial owners of legal-entity customers: each individual owning 25 percent or more of equity interests and one individual with significant responsibility to control the entity.

items.title: US OFAC sanctions compliance and BSA suspicious activity reporting
items.text: US persons must not deal with sanctioned parties and should screen against OFAC lists; banks must file suspicious activity reports generally within 30 calendar days of initial detection of facts that may constitute a basis for filing.
